## 2
I don't think that holds up, and I'm happy to say why. The faked-photos claim has to explain a lot: every astronaut from competing Cold War nations, thousands of satellites that companies and amateurs track daily, GPS that only works because of orbital geometry, and the fact that you can watch ships disappear hull-first over the horizon from a beach. You can test the curvature yourself without trusting any photo. During a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow on the Moon is always round. The only shape that casts a round shadow from every angle is a sphere. What's the piece of evidence that convinced you? I'd rather engage with the strongest version of your reasoning than talk past it.

## 3
Sunlight looks white, but it's actually a mix of all colors, each traveling as a wave. Blue light travels in shorter, tighter waves than red light.

When sunlight hits our atmosphere, it bumps into countless tiny air molecules. Those molecules scatter the short, blue waves far more than the long, red ones, flinging blue light all over the sky. So when you look up, blue light is arriving at your eyes from every direction at once, and the sky looks blue.

Here's a good follow-up to chew on: at sunset the sky turns red because the light has to travel through much more air to reach you, so almost all the blue gets scattered away before it arrives, leaving the reds and oranges.

## 4
雨在深夜落下来，起初只是细碎的声响，后来渐渐密了，敲在窗玻璃上，也敲在楼下的铁皮棚顶。路灯还亮着，灯光被雨水揉碎，在湿漉漉的柏油路上铺成一片摇晃的黄。偶尔有车驶过，轮胎碾过积水，溅起一道长长的水痕，又很快归于寂静。屋檐下的水珠连成线，一滴接一滴地垂落。我靠在窗边，看不清远处的楼，只听见雨声把整座城市包了起来，温吞，绵长，像一句没有说完的话。
